blocked.name: Cooked rice
blocking: Bibimbap does not earn its row as written. Its grain, prep and liquid cells are identical to Gohan's, and its only distinguishing chips ('topped', 'mixed at the table') are things that happen after the rice is cooked — which the note itself concedes ('Nothing at all is done to the rice'). It also breaks the standfirst's promise that 'none of these is a variation on any of the others', because as chipped it is exactly gohan plus toppings. Fix by making the row the version that is a different answer: rename to 'Dolsot bibimbap' and set cook to ["left alone", "lid on", "crust wanted", "topped", "mixed at the table"], so the stone bowl's nurungji becomes a decision in the table rather than an aside in the note. (This also makes blocking item 3 resolve itself.) Alternative if you would rather not stretch bibimbap: replace the row with Cantonese clay-pot rice, which is already named in the crust note and has no row.

'crust wanted' is placed last in every cook cell, after dish-specific chips, so the trie never forks on it and the fourth decision the standfirst promises is invisible in the 'By handling' tree. Today Jollof reads 'sealed with foil — crust wanted', Thieboudienne reads 'crust wanted', Arroz reads 'turned once — crust wanted' — three siblings, three separate branches. Reorder every cook cell as [agitation, cover, crust, extras]: Jollof ["left alone","lid on","crust wanted","sealed with foil"]; Arroz con gandules ["left alone","lid on","crust wanted","turned once"]; Thieboudienne unchanged ["left alone","lid on","crust wanted"]; Paella ["left alone","uncovered","crust wanted","spread thin"]; Chelow ["drained","crust wanted","steamed under a cloth"]. I ran this through the real tree builder: it produces 'left alone > lid on > crust wanted > {Jollof rice, Thieboudienne, Arroz con gandules}', which is the fork the family is about.

The 'On the crust' note says 'in six of these dishes it is the point'. The table has five rows carrying 'crust wanted': Paella, Chelow, Jollof rice, Thieboudienne, Arroz con gandules. Either make the sixth real (see blocking item 1 — dolsot bibimbap) or change the number to five.

'On washing' contradicts the table it sits beside. It says 'Where the ideal is a bound, creamy dish — risotto, paella, congee — the starch is kept and put to work', but Congee's prep chip is "washed". Risotto and paella are 'not washed' and prove the point; congee does not, because its body comes from an hour of collapse rather than from surface starch. Drop congee from that sentence (or, if you believe congee should be unwashed here, change the chip — but then the congee note needs to say why).

Arroz con gandules: the note says 'Uncovered until the liquid is gone, one turn of the spoon, then the lid goes on and stays on', but the cook cell is ["left alone","lid on","turned once","crust wanted"] with no 'uncovered' anywhere. As the table stands, a reader comparing it with Paella (which does carry 'uncovered') would conclude arroz is covered throughout. Either add the phase to the chips — e.g. ["left alone","uncovered at first","turned once","lid on","crust wanted"] — or cut the uncovered stage from the note. The chips are the thing the tree reads, so I would fix the chips.

Jollof rice: the note ends 'Parboiled long-grain is usual, because it survives the braise without breaking', but the row's chips are grain ["long-grain"] and prep ["washed"]. Worse, 'parboiled' already appears in this table as a prep chip on Chelow and Biryani, where it means the cook parboils the rice herself — a different operation from buying converted rice. Put it in the grain column where it belongs (grain: ["long-grain","parboiled"]) and make the note say 'factory-parboiled', or drop the sentence.

Boiled rice's region cell ["South Asia","Caribbean"] renders in the 'By region' tree as 'South Asia > Caribbean — Boiled rice', i.e. the Caribbean drawn as a subdivision of South Asia. This happens because 'South Asia' is shared with Kheer, Pulao and Biryani, so the second chip becomes a child node beneath it. Give this dish a single region chip — "Worldwide" fits its own note ('Most of the world's rice is cooked this way') and reads correctly as its own root. (Khao niao, Nasi lemak and Jollof are unaffected: neither of their region chips is shared, so those collapse to a single line.)
reasons: File reviewed: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/rice.json (16 dishes, 5 facets, 3 nestings). I rebuilt the trie from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts in a scratch script and rendered all three nestings, so every claim below is about what the page will actually draw, not about the JSON in the abstract.

Check 1 (uniqueness) — no two rows are identical, and only one pair is close: Gohan and Bibimbap match on grain, prep and liquid and differ only in `cook`. That is the one place the tree draws two dishes on a shared branch ('measured liquid > water > left alone > lid on'), and the chips that separate them are 'topped' and 'mixed at the table' — assembly, not a decision about cooking the grain. See blocking item 1.

Check 2 (dead dimensions) — none. grain has 13 distinct cells, prep 10, liquid 15, cook 15, region 14. Even prep, where 'washed' appears in 14 of 16 rows, earns its column: 'not washed' (risotto, paella), the three toasting chips and 'parboiled' all fork the tree.

Check 3 (compound chips) — clean. The only chip containing a conjunction is 'tomato and pepper stew', which is one liquid, not two moves. No commas, no 'and then', no chip smuggling in a second decision.

Check 4 (multi-chip ordering) — right in `liquid`, wrong in `cook`. Liquid is consistently quantity-first ('measured liquid' 9x, 'excess water' 3x, 'far more liquid than grain' 2x) then substance, which is why the by-liquid tree forks cleanly and Pulao/Paella meet at 'stock'. `cook` puts 'crust wanted' last in all five rows that have it, after dish-specific chips, so the tree can never fork on it. See blocking item 2.

Check 5 (parent) — correctly absent, and it should stay absent. The Thieboudienne note asserts descent ('the dish jollof descends from, and not a version of it'), but jollof is not thieboudienne-plus-something in the way vodka sauce is rosa-plus-two-things: different grain, different liquid, different origin story. Prose is the right home for it. Worth knowing before anyone is tempted: canonTree() switches the WHOLE family to lineage mode if any single dish has a `parent` (src/lib/canon.ts, `if (canon.dishes.some((d) => d.parent))`), and CanonViews.tsx then hides the nesting switch — one parent link would cost this family all three readings.

Check 6 (coverage) — genuinely global, not one continent in a global hat: Japan, Korea, China, Laos/NE Thailand, Malaysia/Singapore, South Asia, Uzbekistan, Iran, Northern Italy, Valencia, Nigeria/Ghana, Senegal, Puerto Rico. Africa gets two dishes and the older one (thieboudienne) is correctly the parent of the more famous one. South Asia carries 4 of 16, which is the only lopsided count and is defensible.

Check 7 (names and facts) — Gohan, Khao niao, Congee, Kheer, Nasi lemak, Pulao, Plov, Risotto, Paella, Chelow, Biryani, Jollof, Thieboudienne, Arroz con gandules all check out, as do zirvak, devzira, socarrat, tahdig, pegao, xoon and nurungji. Four contradictions between a note and its own row are listed in blocking items 3-6.

Check 8 (standfirst) — it names four decisions and does not praise the food, which is what the check asks. But 'every rice dish on earth' overclaims: fried rice, tahchin, arancini and vinegared sushi rice all start from already-cooked rice, which the root ('Rice, water and heat') rightly excludes. Suggest scoping it — 'every pot of rice on earth', or 'four decisions, and the answers are these' — rather than defending a universal.

Non-blocking, grain vocabulary is inconsistent in a column the tree forks on: 'short-grain japonica' is one chip while risotto and paella use 'short-grain' + variety, so japonica never groups with the other short grains; Pulao is 'basmati' alone while Biryani is 'long-grain' + 'basmati'; 'broken basmati' (kheer) vs 'broken rice' (thieboudienne). Suggest normalising to [class, variety] throughout — and for Chelow, 'aromatic' is an attribute where every other second chip is a cultivar; sadri, domsiah or tarom would be the true parallel.

Non-blocking, 'On one word travelling': polow/pilaf is usually traced through Persian back to Sanskrit pulāka, so 'a single Persian word' is a simplification of a claim the note makes quite forcefully. 'Persian by the time it travelled, with older roots' would survive a reader who looks it up.

Non-blocking, worth considering: Cantonese clay-pot rice is named in the crust note but has no row, and it is a real set of answers (measured liquid, uncovered finish, oil down the sides, toppings steamed on top, crust wanted) rather than a variation on anything already in the table.

blocked.name: Flatbread
blocking: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - Paratha's "parent": "Chapati" silently destroys all three nestings. canonTree (src/lib/canon.ts:109) reads `if (canon.dishes.some((d) => d.parent)) return byLineage(...)` and ignores the nesting argument entirely, and CanonViews.tsx:26/47 hides the Nest selector whenever any dish has a parent. So the outline and staircase do not render 'By leavening', 'By heat' or 'By region' - they render a flat list of 15 top-level dishes with Paratha indented under Chapati, and the three authored readings become dead data. Fix: delete the "parent": "Chapati" line from Paratha. The facets already fork the two apart ('smeared with fat', 'folded', 'rolled again' + 'shallow-fried in ghee'), so nothing is lost. This also settles check 5, which the file currently fails on its own terms: Puri's note says it is 'the chapati's dough sent to a different heat' - the same descent claim as Paratha's - yet Puri carries no parent. Either both are lineage or neither is, and given the cost, neither.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - the root and the standfirst are falsified by the last row of their own table. Root reads 'Ground grain and water, flattened, cooked against direct heat' and the standfirst opens 'Ground grain, water, and something hot to press it against', but Socca's note says 'No grain in it at all'. Widen both: root to 'Ground grain or pulse, water, flattened, cooked against direct heat', standfirst to 'Ground grain or pulse, water, and something hot to press it against.' The 'On the grain' note already makes this the point, so the trunk should admit it.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - standfirst: 'Every settled agricultural people arrived at this' is not true and is the kind of absolute a reader can falsify in one move. Japan, Korea and most of maritime Southeast Asia are settled agricultural societies that steamed whole grain and built no ground-grain flatbread tradition; the Andes went to boiled and freeze-dried tubers; the Caribbean and Amazon made casabe, which is a flatbread but from cassava, not grain. Rewrite to something defensible - e.g. 'Wherever grain was ground and there was a hot surface, someone arrived at this' - and keep the second half, which is the good half.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - the Lavash note contradicts the source the family cites for it. Wikipedia's Lavash article (listed in sources) states plainly that leavened and unleavened forms both exist, and names the Armenian sourdough starter (ttkhmor); the note asserts lavash is 'the same clay wall as naan with the yeast taken out'. The 'unleavened' chip is a fair editorial choice for the thin keeping bread, but the prose must stop stating it as definitional. Rewrite along the lines of: 'The same clay wall as naan. Leavened versions exist, but the thin keeping kind is made without - rolled thin enough that it dries to a cracker...'.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - Corn tortilla note: 'Nixtamalisation ... is the only step in this table that changes the grain's chemistry' is contradicted by two other rows and by the leavening note sitting a screen below it. Days of ersho fermentation in Injera and an overnight wild ferment in Dosa change the chemistry of teff and of rice and urad dal (pH, phytates, starch), and Arepa's masarepa is precooked, which gelatinises its starch. Rewrite to a claim that survives its neighbours - e.g. 'Nixtamalisation - simmering the maize in lime water - is the only alkaline treatment here, and the only step that changes the grain before it is ever a dough.' The niacin and gluten-free cohesion sentences are correct and should stay.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/flatbread.json - Msemen note: 'Paratha and laobing do the same thing, and none of the three learned it from the others' asserts independent invention where a continuous chain is documented. Katlama/qatlama - dough rolled thin, smeared with fat, folded or coiled, fried - runs as katmer in Turkey, qatlama in Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, kattama in Kyrgyzstan, gambir in Mongolia, and katlama in Kashmir and Pakistan, and is routinely described as the same thing as paratha and roti canai. That belt bridges the Maghreb-to-China gap the sentence claims is empty. Either cut the independence claim or replace it with the true and more interesting fact - e.g. 'Paratha and laobing do the same thing, and a belt of layered breads called katlama runs most of the way between them.' (Note that the Dosa note's 'reached independently' about injera is a much safer claim and can stand.)
reasons: Checks 1-3 pass cleanly. No two rows are identical, and in fact no two rows differ in only one cell either - every pair of the 16 dishes differs in at least two dimensions. No column is decoration: leaven has 8 distinct cell values, grain 10, flatten 16, cook 13, region 15. No chip is a compound - nothing contains a comma or an 'and', and the genuinely double answers are split correctly ('rice' + 'urad dal', 'oven' + 'on a bed of hot pebbles').

Check 4 passes on the two facets that carry the nestings. Every multi-chip leaven cell leads with the shared value ('unleavened' before 'no fermentation at all' on Matzo, 'fermented batter' before 'wild ersho starter' on Injera, 'chemical' before 'a little baking powder' on Flour tortilla), and every cook cell leads with the surface. I ran the trie in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts over this data: 'By heat' forks exactly where the family wants it to - Naan and Lavash meet under 'tandoor - slapped on the wall', Pita and Matzo under 'oven - very hot floor', Laobing and Msemen under 'shallow-fried in oil', and the two tortillas under 'dry comal'. That reading is the best thing in the file, which is why the parent bug below matters so much.

'By region' is nearly flat: 12 of the 16 dishes come out as top-level leaves and only 'South Asia' forks. The region vocabulary mixes scales and orderings - Msemen goes narrow-to-broad ('Morocco', 'Maghreb'), Corn tortilla goes broad-to-narrow ('Mesoamerica', 'Mexico'), Lavash alternates ('Armenia', 'Caucasus', 'Iran'). Since the trie forks on the leading chip, a rule of 'broadest shared unit first' would make this reading work. Concretely, the two tortillas - the pair the flour tortilla note explicitly pairs - never meet: they would if Corn tortilla were ["Mexico", "Mesoamerica"] and Flour tortilla ["Mexico", "Northern Mexico", "US Southwest"]. Same issue: Chapati's 'East Africa' and Injera's 'Ethiopia'/'Eritrea' name one place at two scales, so the three Iranian breads (Sangak, and Naan and Lavash which carry Iran as a trailing chip) never gather either. Not blocking, but 'By region' is currently the weakest of the three readings.

Check 6 passes - the coverage is not parochial. Sixteen rows across South Asia (4), the Iranian plateau and Caucasus (2), the Levant and the Jewish diaspora (2), the Horn of Africa (1), the Maghreb (1), South India (1), Mesoamerica and the US Southwest (2), northern South America (1), northern China (1), and the Ligurian coast (1). Wheat is 11 of 16, which the 'On the grain' note names rather than hides.

Check 7: most of it holds up. I verified against the cited sources - sangak does mean pebble and is a wholemeal sourdough baked on stones and lifted off with a hook; matzah's eighteen minutes does run from the flour getting wet, and the perforations are there 'to keep the finished product from puffing up', exactly as the note says; laobing is described as unleavened, pan-fried, pizza-sized and chewy in northern China; masarepa is real and did collapse a day's work. The tandoor figures (around 400C, off the wall in ninety seconds) and the count of five leavening answers are both right. Four claims do not hold, and they are in blocking.

Two smaller things worth a pass. Fat in the dough is invisible in the grid even though three notes turn on it - paratha's ghee, flour tortilla's lard, naan's yoghurt - whereas the exemplar carries exactly this on its dough facet ('enriched with fat'); the Flattened column only records fat as a lamination move ('smeared with fat'), so the flour tortilla's lard is asserted in prose and nowhere in the table. And Socca's pan appears in two columns at once ('into a hot pan' under Flattened, 'in a copper pan' under Cooked).

Flattened is the only facet never offered as a nesting, and it is the most discriminating column in the table (16 distinct cells, but real chip-level forks: 'rolled thin' x8, 'poured as batter' x3, 'stretched by hand' x3). A fourth nesting {"label": "By shaping", "by": ["flatten", "cook"]} would sort the family into rolled / stretched / poured / pressed / patted, which is a genuinely different question from leavening or heat. Optional.

Minor vocabulary drift in the grain column: Chapati and Paratha carry 'wholemeal atta' while Sangak carries 'wholemeal' for the same idea. Harmless while grain sits last in the nesting order, but it costs a fork if grain is ever promoted.

blocked.name: Noodle soup
blocking: Niurou mian's broth cell leads with 'clear' while its own note says 'the broth is dark where Lanzhou's is clear'. The first chip of `broth` is the family's primary axis, so the table and the note disagree on the one decision the family is built around. Fix by giving it its own first chip — ['dark', 'beef bones', 'soy-braised', 'doubanjiang'] — which also stops it sharing the 'clear' branch with Lanzhou in the default tree, the exact contrast the note is drawing.

Kalguksu's broth cell asserts both 'clear' (chip 1) and 'clouded by noodle starch' (chip 4), so it files under the clear branch while saying it is not clear. Either lead with 'clouded' ['clouded', 'dried anchovy', 'kelp', 'thickened by the noodle'] or drop the fourth chip and leave the clouding to the note and to note 3, which already explains it. It cannot be both in the same cell.

Phở bò is tagged region Hanoi but given a 'herb plate' at the table, and note 2 builds its whole argument on that plate. Hanoi phở arrives essentially bare — spring onion, maybe quẩy, with chilli sauce, lime and pickled garlic on the table; the plate of Thai basil, sawtooth coriander and bean sprouts is the Saigon service. Either change region to ['Vietnam', 'Saigon'] or drop 'herb plate' from `finish` and rewrite the phở half of note 2. As written the row is wrong about the city it names.

Curry laksa's region ['Malaysia', 'Singapore'] renders in the By region tree as 'Malaysia > Singapore' — Singapore nested inside Malaysia as if it were a locality of it. Every other row uses country-then-place (Japan > Tokyo, China > Gansu). Pick one bowl: ['Malaysia', 'Kuala Lumpur'] or plain ['Malaysia']. This also fixes the noodle cell, which currently merges two different dishes — Malaysian curry mee is thin rice vermicelli plus yellow wheat noodles, while the thick round rice noodle is Katong laksa in Singapore, which does not mix wheat in. Choose one and make the noodle chips match.

Bún bò Huế's noodle reads ['rice','round','thick'] where curry laksa and asam laksa read ['rice','thick','round']. Same three chips, opposite order, so the trie splits an identical noodle into two branches — under By noodle you get 'rice > round > thick — Bún bò Huế' sitting beside a separate 'rice > thick > round' fork. Reorder Bún bò Huế to ['rice','thick','round'] so the three thick round rice noodles fork together.

The root, 'Noodles in a bowl, with hot broth poured over', and the standfirst's opening 'Boil noodles, pour hot broth over them' are contradicted by two members: kalguksu's noodles are boiled in the soup (note 3 celebrates exactly that: 'The noodle is an ingredient in the broth') and ash reshteh's are cooked in the pot too. Reword the root to something both halves satisfy — e.g. 'Noodles and hot broth in one bowl' — and open the standfirst with 'Cook noodles, get hot broth onto them, put something on top.'

Rename the Taiwanese row. 'Niurou mian' and 'Lanzhou beef lamian' are the same words — 牛肉麵 — so the table has two rows whose names collide for any reader who knows either. Use 'Hongshao niurou mian' or 'Taiwanese beef noodle soup'.

Lanzhou beef lamian's note is factually wrong about the mechanism: 'the beef is sliced thin and added at the end rather than stewed in it'. The beef is simmered in that pot — it is where the broth's flavour comes from — then lifted, sliced and laid on the bowl at serving. Clarity comes from a bare simmer and relentless skimming (the chip 'skimmed until transparent' already says this), not from keeping the meat out. Rewrite along the lines of: 'Judged on the clarity of the broth, which is why the pot is skimmed and never allowed to boil — the beef cooks in it, then comes out to be sliced and laid on at the end.'
reasons: Checks 1-3 pass. I rebuilt the trie from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts against /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/noodle-soup.json: no two dishes share an identical row; no dimension is constant (broth 5 first-chip values, noodle 3, finish 2, region 12, top 15); no chip is a comma- or 'and'-joined compound.

Check 5 passes. `parent` is correctly absent — no bowl here is another bowl plus a step, and note 4 ('Why nothing here has a parent') says so explicitly and correctly. Taiwanese braised beef noodle is not descended from Lanzhou lamian, and asam laksa is not curry laksa minus coconut.

Check 4 mostly passes — broth and noodle cells lead with the shared move, and the derived tree forks cleanly (clear > beef bones > five dishes; wheat > alkaline > three ramen/wonton). One cell breaks it (see blocking) and one facet does no structural work: with nesting ['broth','noodle','top'] the third level never forks, because 15 of 16 'top' cells begin with a unique chip. Dropping 'top' from that nesting produces an identical tree.

The 'finish' dimension — the standfirst's stated second argument, and the subject of a whole note — appears in no nesting, so a reader can never read the table that way. Recommend adding {label: 'By who finishes it', by: ['finish','broth']}; it forks 5 (arrives finished) against 11 (finished by the eater) at the top level, which is exactly the argument the standfirst promises.

Check 6: coverage leans but does not fail — 13 of 16 bowls are Asian, with only Ashkenazi Europe/US and New Orleans outside. Nothing is wrong with what is there, but the global label would be better earned by one or two of: sopa de fideo (Mexico — would add 'tomato' to the broth vocabulary, a fifth answer nothing else covers), tortellini in brodo (Italy — clear capon broth, filled noodle), thukpa (Tibet/Nepal), lagman (Uyghur/Central Asia).

Check 7: names, diacritics and regions are otherwise right — Phở bò, Bún bò Huế, Huế, Fukuoka/Hakata for tonkotsu, Gansu for Lanzhou, Guangdong for wonton noodle, Penang for asam laksa, Chiang Mai for khao soi, Java for soto ayam. Ingredient chips check out: dried flounder and dried shrimp in the Cantonese broth, asam gelugor as 'dried garcinia', hae ko as 'thick prawn paste', huyết as 'cubed pork blood', yangnyeomjang as 'seasoned soy dressing', kaedama as 'a second helping of noodles'.

Check 8: the standfirst is specific rather than admiring, and the four notes each carry a real mechanism. Two small gaps — it lists four broth answers but the vocabulary has five (nothing points at 'thickened', which is what makes mohinga and ash reshteh different), and its opening premise is contradicted by two rows (see blocking).

Minor, non-blocking: the Tonkotsu note opens 'Same bones as a clear stock' directly beneath a row whose clear stock is chicken bones, so it reads as a comparison to shoyu ramen when it means pork bones generically. 'Same pork bones a clear stock would use' removes the trip.

blocked.name: Raw and cured fish
blocking: Poke's chips contradict Poke's own note. The dress cell lists 'soy sauce' while the note says the dish is 'older than the soy-and-sesame bowl it became' and names sea salt, limu and inamona as the real dressing. Confirmed: shoyu arrived with Japanese plantation labour and the modern form dates to roughly the 1970s. Pick one — either drop 'soy sauce' from dress (salt is already carried by the cure chip 'salted at the plate', leaving limu seaweed + inamona), or rewrite the note to describe the modern bowl. As it stands the row asserts one dish and the note asserts another.

Crudo and Aguachile have the same decision path. Both are acid [citrus juice, dressed at the plate] + cure [salted at the plate] + cut [sliced across the grain, paper-thin], so in a feature that defines dishes by what separates them, these two arrive at the same leaf under both 'By acid' and 'By cure'. Fix on one of the three tree facets, not on dress. Cleanest option: change Aguachile's cure to a new chip 'salted in the liquid' — true (the salt goes into the chile water, not onto the plated fish) and it creates a real fork under citrus > dressed at the plate. Alternative: give Aguachile cut ['butterflied', 'opened flat'], which matches its own note's 'classically butterflied shrimp' and separates it from every sliced dish in the table.

The note titled 'On the Pacific and the ninth name' refers to nothing a reader can locate. The body names four dishes (kokoda, ʻota ʻika, oka iʻa, poisson cru), and kokoda is the eleventh entry in the dish list, not the ninth. Whatever the phrase counted in an earlier draft is gone. Retitle to what the note actually argues — e.g. 'On one dish under four flags' — and keep the body, which is the best guard against the false-cognate reading in the whole family.

Spellings to correct. 'inamona' should be 'ʻinamona' with the ʻokina — the entry already uses the ʻokina correctly for 'ʻOta ʻika' in sources, so the table is inconsistent with itself. 'Hoe-deopbap' should be 'Hoedeopbap' under Revised Romanization (the hyphen is not standard and the parent field, note and source label can stay as they are).

'tossed at the table' is in the Dressed column but it is a serving move, not a dressing — it is the only chip in sixteen rows that is not something laid on the fish, and it silently breaks the column's meaning. The Yusheng note already makes the point better ('the only dish here whose serving move is the dish'), so delete the chip. Yusheng still reads cleanly on plum sauce and shredded vegetables. (Tiradito's 'no onion' is fine by contrast — it is a decision, and it matches the negation vocabulary of 'no acid' and 'no cure' used elsewhere.)
reasons: Check 1 (duplicate rows): no two dishes are identical across all five facets. But Crudo and Aguachile are identical on all three tree-forming facets — acid [citrus juice, dressed at the plate], cure [salted at the plate], cut [sliced across the grain, paper-thin] — so under both 'By acid' and 'By cure' they land in the same leaf with nothing separating them. They differ only in dress and region, which is the decorative end of the table. See blocking.

Check 2 (dead dimensions): every facet takes multiple values and none is constant. Acid runs no acid / citrus / vinegar plus a real duration ladder (dressed at the plate → minutes → hours → days); cure runs no cure / salted at the plate / packed in salt / brined in salt; cut runs sliced-across-the-grain / cubes / cured-whole. Dress is the most discriminating column (every dish differs) but appears in no nesting — that is fine, it reads as leaf detail rather than decoration.

Check 3 (compound chips): chips are atomic. 'mustard and dill sauce' is one named sauce (hovmästarsås), not two things, and 'chile blitzed with lime' is one preparation. 'shredded vegetables' and 'sweet potato alongside' are single chips. Nothing here needs splitting.

Check 4 (lead chips): the ordering discipline holds across all sixteen rows without exception — acid always leads with the acid type then the duration, cure always leads with the cure type then the modifier, cut always leads with the geometry (sliced across the grain / cut in cubes / cured whole) then the refinement. All three nestings fork cleanly on the first chip.

Check 5 (parent): used twice and both are real. Hoe-deopbap genuinely is hoe re-served over rice, and the cube-versus-ribbon reasoning is the best single note in the family. Tiradito genuinely descends from ceviche via Nikkei cooking. Correctly withheld from kinilaw, kokoda and poke, and the 'On the Pacific' note makes that restraint explicit rather than leaving it to chance.

Check 6 (parochial): not parochial. East Asia (Japan x2, Korea x2), Southeast Asia (Singapore/Malaysia, Philippines), the Pacific (Hawaii, Fiji), Latin America (Peru x2, Mexico), and both ends of Europe (Italy, Spain, Germany, Netherlands, Sweden/Norway). Optional only: nothing from the Middle East or Africa — Turkish/Greek lakerda would slot in as brined-and-sliced next to mojama, though it may be too close to earn a row.

Check 7 (facts): I verified the load-bearing claims. Kokoda's coconut cream as a ~1930s Suva restaurant addition checks out (Tourism Fiji attributes it to a Suva restaurateur around then), as does walu, lime and seawater as the older form. The Butuan balangay dig — halved tabon-tabon husks with cut fish bones, c. 10th–13th century — supports 'roughly a thousand years back' and the pre-Spanish point. Matjes gibbing is right: the pancreas is deliberately retained and its enzymes drive the autolytic ripening. Poke's older form as salt, limu and roasted kukui nut on aku is right, and shoyu is confirmed as the post-contact addition — which is exactly why the poke row contradicts itself (see blocking). Shime saba's salt-then-vinegar order and its reason are correct. Gravlax, mojama, rollmops, tiradito, aguachile, hoe and yusheng all read accurately.

Check 8 (standfirst): it makes falsifiable claims rather than praising the food. 'Crudo and ceviche are about ninety seconds apart. Ceviche and gravlax are three days apart' states the family's actual thesis — that the axis is time — and both numbers are defensible. No adjectives about deliciousness anywhere. This is the strongest part of the entry.

Nit, non-blocking: matjes 'ripened for days'. The EU spec for Hollandse maatjesharing gives four hours to four days depending on the fish, so 'days' sits at the top of the range. 'Ripened in the barrel' would be safer and loses nothing.

Nit, non-blocking: shime saba 'hours in the acid' against 'drawn for an hour' in the cure. The common Japanese method is the reverse ratio — salt 1–3 hours, vinegar 20–60 minutes — with multi-hour vinegar reserved for firmer sabazushi styles. Both exist, so the row is defensible, but worth a deliberate decision rather than an accident, since this row is billed as the hinge of the family.

Nit, non-blocking: crudo's 'Sashimi's Mediterranean sibling, not its descendant' is half right. The southern Italian raw-seafood tradition is genuinely indigenous, but crudo as a plated restaurant genre owes a great deal to sashimi. 'Not only its descendant' would survive scrutiny; the flat denial slightly overclaims.

Nit, non-blocking: aguachile is classically shrimp, not fish, inside a family whose root is 'A fish that never meets heat'. The note is honest about this, so it holds — but it is the one row where the root sentence does not quite cover the dish.

Nit, non-blocking: the 1930s coconut-cream date and the Butuan dating are the two most specific claims in the entry and neither has a matching entry in sources (kokoda is covered only by the ʻOta ʻika link). Adding a Fiji source and the Kinilaw article would close that gap. There is also no source for shime saba or crudo.

blocked.name: Food on a skewer
blocking: FIRE CHIP ORDER — this one breaks a claim the family makes about itself. 'narrow trough grill' sits at position 1 for Chuanr and Arrosticini but at position 2 for Yakitori (behind 'binchōtan'), so in the 'By fire' tree the three trough grills cannot fork together — which is exactly what the note 'On what the stick is actually for' asserts ('the Japanese konro, the Xinjiang charcoal channel and the Abruzzese canala are the same idea three times over'). The tree contradicts the prose. Position 2 of `fire` must always be grill geometry, never fuel refinement. Fix: Yakitori fire -> ["charcoal","narrow trough grill","binchōtan"]; Satay fire -> ["charcoal","open grill","coconut shell","fanned by hand"] (or whatever geometry is true for a satay brazier — it must not lead with the fuel). The 'wood embers' branch already does this correctly, so charcoal is the only inconsistent branch.

SALT SPELLED FOUR WAYS in `prep` position 1: Chuanr 'salted', Arrosticini 'salted at the fire', Churrasco 'coarse salt only', Espetada 'coarse salt'. Three dishes whose shared move is 'the only thing on it is salt' each get their own singleton twig under 'no marinade', so the tree cannot fork on the thing they have in common. Fix: lead all three with the same chip and demote the qualifier — Chuanr ["no marinade","salted"], Churrasco ["no marinade","salted","coarse"], Arrosticini ["no marinade","salted","at the fire"]. Yakitori then correctly stands alone on 'raw onto the stick', which is the real distinction.

COVERAGE GAP: no Iran, and no Levant. Sixteen dishes, a dedicated note titled 'On calling it all kebab', and the tradition that gave the word to every other entry is absent while Turkey appears twice. This is the one place the coverage is indefensible. Add at least one Persian row. Best choice is Kabab kubideh, because it earns forks in two nestings rather than sitting alone: thread ["ground meat","minced lamb","pressed onto a flat blade"] (forks with Seekh kebab on 'minced lamb'), prep ["seasoned into the mince","grated onion","turmeric","salt"], fire ["charcoal","mangal","skewers on rails","turned constantly"] (forks with Adana), sauce ["after the cooking","grilled tomato alongside","butter into the rice"] (a deliberate rhyme against Adana's 'butter into the flatbread'), region ["Iran"]. Optional second: Jujeh kabab — thread ["cubes of meat","bone-in chicken","flat metal skewer"], prep ["wet marinade","saffron","onion juice","lemon"], fire ["charcoal","mangal","skewers on rails"], sauce ["during the cooking","basted with saffron butter"], region ["Iran"].

CHURRASCO IS NOT A DISH NAME at this altitude — it names Brazil's whole barbecue tradition (and in Spanish America, a grilled steak with no skewer at all). The row actually describes picanha no espeto. Brochette's note already owns exactly this problem for itself ('The word is only French for skewer, which is how a generic became a dish name'); churrasco has the same problem and no acknowledgement. Either rename the dish to 'Picanha no espeto' (which also stops it reading as a near-twin of Espetada), or add a clause to its note saying the word names the tradition and this is its skewer form.

NO NESTING EXPOSES DURING-VS-AFTER, despite the note 'On during or after' treating it as the family's central decision. Under the default 'By marinade' order [prep, sauce, fire], the position-1 prep chips are dish-unique, so every path dead-ends before the sauce facet is ever reached — the during/after axis is collapsed into a label and never forks anything. Add a fourth nesting: { "label": "By when the sauce arrives", "by": ["sauce", "prep"] }. That puts the three-way fork (during the cooking / after the cooking / none) at the top where the note argues it belongs, and 'sumac onion alongside' still forks Şiş kebap against Adana beneath it.

SKEWER-MATERIAL VOCABULARY is inconsistent and one chip is incomplete. 'thin bamboo' (Yakitori, Satay, Souvlaki, Anticucho, Sosatie) and 'thin wooden skewer' (Arrosticini) are the same move under two names — pick one. And Suya's 'thin flat skewer' is the only skewer chip in the family that names no material, while every other one does ('flat metal skewer', 'long metal shampur', 'bay laurel stick', 'thin bamboo'); it reads as metal by proximity to Chuanr's flat metal, when suya is grilled on wooden sticks. Make it explicit either way.
reasons: File under review: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/skewer.json. After any edit, run `node /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/scripts/build-canon.mjs` to regenerate src/data/canon-families.ts.
Check 1 passes: all 16 dishes have unique facet signatures across all five dimensions — no row is another row written twice.

Check 2 passes: every dimension varies. thread 5 leading values, prep 4, fire 4, sauce 3, region 16. Nothing is decoration. (Minor: the 'By region' nesting is near-flat — only Turkey has two members, so 14 of 16 dishes are singleton twigs. Same shape as the dough-with-filling exemplar, so I'm treating it as house style, not a defect.)
Check 3 passes: no chip is two things joined by a comma or 'and'. Every chip is one move.

Check 5 is right as authored: no `parent` anywhere, and that is correct. Sosatie's descent from sate is etymological, not compositional — it shares neither meat, marinade, fire nor sauce with satay, so it is a cousin, not a child. Worth knowing before anyone is tempted: canonTree() switches the WHOLE family to lineage mode if any single dish has a parent (src/lib/canon.ts, `if (canon.dishes.some((d) => d.parent))`), which would silently discard all three nestings and flatten the other 15 dishes to root. The third note, 'On calling it all kebab', already argues the case in prose.

Check 8 passes: the standfirst is mechanical, not praise — it names what the stick does (turns a handful as one, fixes distance from the coals) and then names the actual axes of variation. Two small things: it claims 'Every fire-using culture worked this out independently' where the exemplar hedges with 'Nearly every' — consider matching. And its first sentence makes the stick the subject, but the stick is the LAST chip in every `thread` cell and so never forks any tree; the standfirst's own three-item list quietly drops it.

Check 7, names and spellings, is in good shape. Verified correct: Şiş kebap, Adana kebabı, binchōtan, tare, shampur, tkemali, ají panca, yaji, zırh-minced lamb with tail fat on a flat blade, castrato mutton for arrosticini, pau de louro (bay laurel stick) for espetada, Cape Malay sosatie, tandoor-hung seekh and tikka, picanha folded on a sword skewer, sumac onion with both Turkish entries. Regions all check out, including Punjab for chicken tikka and Abruzzo for arrosticini.

Two factual hedges worth considering, not blocking: Chuanr as 'no marinade / salted' is true of the Xinjiang street version but restaurant chuanr is usually marinated — the note half-owns this already. And Souvlaki's 'thin bamboo' is commercially true but traditionally the skewer is plain wood.

Non-blocking structural note: because prep, sauce and thread all carry dish-unique chips from position 1 onward, any facet placed early in a nesting dead-ends immediately. That is why 'By marinade' gives four clean top branches and then singletons. That is acceptable — the top-level fork is the valuable part — but it is the reason blocking item 5 matters.
